1320.bp: When you search on Netflix or Amazon for something to watch, the system quietly learns what you like by watching which titles you click on, rate, or watch. But there's a problem: the system only sees the items it has data about (maybe 10,000 movies), and if you search for something rare or new, it's flying blind. This paper tackles that gap using language models, which have seen and read about millions of products and concepts across the internet.
1320.wh: The tension is this: if you just use ID numbers (like 'item 5394'), the system sees no connection between similar things—it's like trying to recognize faces by memorizing a person's ID number instead of their features. If you only use text descriptions (like 'historical drama with subtitles'), you lose the precise collaborative signal that 'users who watched this specific rare documentary also watched that other rare one.' You need both worlds at once, but they conflict: one is sparse and relies on hard-to-find co-viewing patterns, the other is general but can miss the quirky preferences that make recommendations personal.
1320.ap: They build a system with two parallel channels. One channel uses a language model to read the text description of an item ('Oscar-winning French film about a clockmaker in 1920s Paris') and generate rich semantic features. The other channel learns from actual user interactions using ID numbers. They use a mixture-of-experts adapter—think of it as a selective attention mechanism that learns which features matter most for different types of items—to blend these semantic features into sharper representations. Then both channels get aggregated carefully at the end so neither drowns out the other.
1320.ww: This works because language models have seen billions of texts and learned the abstract space of 'what makes things similar'—they know that 'historical drama' and 'period piece' and 'costume film' are close cousins. When you feed a new rare item through this semantic channel, the model immediately situates it in this vast conceptual landscape, even if no one has ever interacted with it. Meanwhile, the ID-based channel still captures the fine-grained collaborative signal (subtle user taste patterns) that can't be inferred from text alone. By using a mixture-of-experts adapter, the system learns which users care more about semantics versus collaborative signals—some users are 'text-ready' (they respond to descriptions), others are purely driven by 'what people like me watched.'
1320.po: The result is a system that handles both sparse, rare items and popular ones gracefully, using both the semantic knowledge built into language models and the collaborative wisdom baked into user interaction patterns. The mixture-of-experts layer ensures these two signals fuse smoothly without one dominating arbitrarily.

1321.bp: When you ask a search engine or AI assistant a complex question like 'Who won the Science Fiction Hugo Award in 2015 and where do they live now?', the system needs to search the web, find multiple pieces of evidence, and piece them together logically. Most AI systems trained today are mediocre at this—they either guess wildly, fail to search strategically, or follow bad search paths that dead-end. This paper aims to build web-browsing AI agents that reliably solve multi-step questions.
1321.wh: The big challenge: existing training data for this is either too simple (questions that only need one or two web searches) or drawn from closed databases like Wikipedia (where you can memorize all the answers). Real-world web questions are open-ended—the answer isn't in any single document, and some paths lead to dead ends. The other problem is that training these agents the traditional way (reinforcement learning where you let them explore and penalize failure) is incredibly slow and unstable because the search space is vast and sparse—most random action sequences fail, so the system rarely sees a success signal to learn from.
1321.ap: They build a two-stage approach. First, they construct a huge synthetic dataset of complex questions by starting with Wikipedia entities, then automatically searching the web to gather evidence, and synthesizing new questions grounded in that evidence—creating a training dataset that looks realistic but is fully verifiable. Second, they train agents in two steps: (1) teach them basic web-browsing moves using supervised learning (here's how an expert searches and clicks), then (2) refine them using a preference-learning approach where they score different search actions offline by checking whether each action led downstream to finding the right answer.
1321.ww: This two-stage approach is smart because it avoids the slow, unstable loop of trial-and-error learning. Instead, you first teach the agent the basic 'vocabulary' of web actions (how to formulate queries, which links to click) through supervised imitation. Then you refine its judgment by comparing past actions retrospectively: if searching for 'Hugo Award 2015 nominees' led to success, that's a good action; if searching for 'science fiction awards history' led to a dead-end, downweight it. This is efficient because you're not waiting for the agent to explore—you're learning from data you already have. The synthetic data ensures questions are verifiable so you can clearly score which search strategies worked.
1321.po: The payoff is agents that reliably solve complex, multi-step questions on the open web without needing expensive trial-and-error training. The model achieves results competitive with human-quality web searches while running much faster than older reinforcement-learning approaches, especially on questions that demand 3-5 separate web searches to triangulate an answer.

1322.bp: Imagine shopping on Amazon where the product page has photos, descriptions, a video walkthrough, and customer reviews in text. All of this is different 'modalities'—different ways of representing the same thing. When you search or get recommendations, the best systems should understand all these angles, not just read the words. This paper asks: how do you build a recommender that handles multiple modalities together?
1322.wh: The problem sounds simple—why not just feed all modalities (text, images, audio if present) into a neural network? But there's a trap: one modality often dominates. Imagine a luxury handbag where the product photo is stunning and informative, but the description is thin. If you train naively, the image modality learns to 'take over' the final representation, and the text signal gets ignored. Or worse, the image and text might disagree—an image shows red leather, but the text says 'available in navy'—and the model doesn't know how to reconcile them. You end up with representations where different modalities aren't actually aligned; they're just jumbled together.
1322.ap: They use a late-fusion strategy, meaning they generate representations separately for each modality (one network processes text descriptions, another processes images), then carefully fuse them at the end rather than mixing everything from the start. To prevent one modality from drowning out others, they add a contrastive alignment layer—a mechanism that penalizes the model if text-based and image-based representations of the same item are far apart in the semantic space. They also add special tokens at the fusion point to preserve the sequential structure that the neural network uses to generate recommendations.
1322.ww: Late fusion works better than early fusion here because it lets each modality develop its own rich understanding before negotiating agreement. Text networks learn to parse language nuance; image networks learn visual patterns. Then the contrastive layer acts as a referee, saying 'your text representation and image representation for this handbag should be nearby in the semantic space—if they're far apart, you're misaligned.' This pulls the two modalities into agreement without forcing one to dominate. The special tokens preserve the sequential integrity of the generation process, ensuring that when the model generates a recommendation, it doesn't lose track of which parts of the representation came from which modality.
1322.po: The result is a system that improves recommendation quality by over 20 percent compared to models that rely on only one modality or naively mash all of them together. Items are represented in a semantically coherent way where text and images agree, leading to recommendations that genuinely reflect the multifaceted nature of real products.

1323.bp: In information retrieval, after you search Google for 'best Italian restaurants near me,' the engine returns a ranked list of hundreds or thousands of candidates. The last step—ranking them in order—is critical. If the #1 result is mediocre, users leave disappointed. A reranker is a second-pass system that takes those top candidates and reorders them more carefully. This paper teaches rerankers to think through their reasoning before deciding which document comes first.
1323.wh: Traditional rerankers see a query and a document, and instantly score them without explaining why—they're like a judge who says 'this brief is better' without stating the reasoning. On complex queries that require interpretation ('Should I buy this laptop for machine learning?'), that scoring often misses what the user really needs. When you move to datasets where queries are tricky and diverse (not the typical Google queries), the system's weak reasoning becomes obvious—it scores the wrong document as #1 because it didn't deeply engage with what the user was asking.
1323.ap: They train an LLM-based reranker using reinforcement learning to generate an intermediate reasoning step. The system reads the query and candidate document, thinks through the match ('This document discusses training speed and GPU compatibility, which are relevant to machine learning work'), then scores them. Crucially, they train this using only relevance labels (answers to 'is this document good?'), not explicit reasoning supervision (they don't need humans to write out the reasoning). The reinforcement learning signal teaches the model: if your reasoning leads to a correct rank ordering, reinforce it; if it leads to a wrong ordering, penalize it.
1323.ww: This works because explicit reasoning acts as an internal checkpoint. When the model writes out its reasoning, it's committing to a line of logic—it can't just score a document high arbitrarily. That commitment forces the model to actually check its logic against the document content. The reinforcement learning signal (whether the final ranking was correct) then propagates backward to improve both the reasoning and the final scoring. On complex queries where shallow similarity matching fails, reasoning-enhanced reranking shines because the model has to articulate what makes a document relevant—and articulation forces precision.
1323.po: The payoff is a reranker that outperforms both simpler prompting-based approaches and supervised fine-tuning on challenging out-of-domain questions. On the BRIGHT benchmark (which requires nuanced reasoning), a smaller 14-billion-parameter version matches the performance of GPT-4-powered baselines while being far cheaper to run, and a larger 32-billion version achieves state-of-the-art performance.

1324.bp: Every time a search engine or e-commerce site ranks results, it processes long sequences of text—a query plus a multi-paragraph product description. This processing is expensive; running fast enough to answer queries within milliseconds requires serious computational efficiency. This paper asks: can you speed up this process without losing ranking quality?
1324.wh: Naive token compression doesn't work well for rerankers, as the authors discovered. If you aggressively group tokens together early (at the embedding layer), you lose fine-grained information that's crucial for nuanced ranking decisions. For example, grouping 'excellent customer service' into one compressed token might lose the distinction that this is praise for service, not product quality—important when ranking restaurant reviews. Dense retrieval systems (which compare one query embedding to one document embedding) tolerate early compression, but cross-encoder rerankers (which look at detailed query-document interactions) suffer from it.
1324.ap: Instead of compressing tokens early, they apply token pooling at middle layers of the transformer network. This means the model processes the full, uncompressed token sequence at first, learning rich interactions between query and document. Then, once the network has built up a good understanding of those interactions, they compress tokens together at intermediate layers. This preserves fine-grained reasoning early while reducing computational cost later. They also show this approach works for large language model-based rerankers that rank many documents at once (listwise ranking).
1324.ww: Layer-wise compression works because it respects the information flow in neural networks. Early layers need rich signal to build nuanced representations—they're doing the hard cognitive work of parsing what the query is asking and what the document offers. Once that semantic understanding is built (by middle layers), you can safely compress—the model has already extracted the high-level concepts. It's like reading a detailed legal document carefully, then summarizing key points once you understand them, rather than summarizing before you read. For long-document ranking, this approach surprisingly makes models trained on short passages work better on long documents—compression regularizes them to focus on the most informative phrases.
1324.po: The result is dramatically faster reranking—25 percent speed-up for ranking passages, up to 116 percent for longer documents—while maintaining or even improving ranking quality. The method is simple enough to apply to different reranker architectures (BERT-based, LLM-based) without retraining from scratch, making it immediately useful for production systems.

1325.bp: On delivery apps like DoorDash, users type queries like 'Wildflower' expecting results to map to relevant categories (restaurant? retail? floral delivery?). The system needs to understand what the user actually wants, not just match text keywords. On a food marketplace with hundreds of categories, mapping queries to the right ones is a fundamental problem that directly affects whether users find what they're looking for.
1325.wh: The tension here is stark: simple keyword matching fails on ambiguous queries. 'Wildflower' could mean a chain restaurant, a home decor product, or flowers. Hand-written rules don't scale to thousands of categories and query types. General-purpose language models can reason ('Wildflower could be a restaurant'), but they hallucinate—they confidently suggest categories that don't exist in the catalog. You need a system that combines reasoning (to understand ambiguous intent) with grounding (to verify that the suggested category actually exists and makes business sense).
1325.ap: They build an agentic system that reasons with multiple information sources. When a user types a query, the system (1) first retrieves candidate categories from a staged pipeline that searches the live catalog, (2) autonomously invokes web search when the query is ambiguous or new (when catalog search returns nothing), and (3) synthesizes an ordered list of multiple possible intents rather than forcing a single answer. A separate disambiguation layer then resolves that list using business rules and policies (e.g., if both restaurant and retail match, prefer restaurant on this app). This decoupled design lets different businesses supply their own grounding sources and rules.
1325.ww: This works because it separates two different cognitive tasks: reasoning about intent (which an LLM is good at) and grounding that reasoning in reality (which retrieval and business rules handle). The LLM reasons 'Wildflower could mean a restaurant or flowers,' but the retrieval layer grounds it: 'our restaurant catalog actually has Wildflower; our floral catalog does not.' When the catalog is silent, agentic web search can quickly gather external context. By emitting multiple intents, the system admits uncertainty (natural for ambiguous queries) and lets business logic make the final call based on domain knowledge.
1325.po: The system achieves a 10.9 percentage-point improvement in accuracy over an ungrounded LLM baseline and 4.6 percentage-points over the legacy production system. On long-tail (rare, unusual) queries, ablations show that catalog grounding alone contributes 8.3 percentage-points, web search adds another 3.2 percentage-points, and the disambiguation layer adds 1.5 percentage-points—each component earning its place through measurable impact.

1326.bp: E-commerce platforms like Trendyol (a large Turkish marketplace) run thousands of experiments weekly: 'Does a red checkout button increase conversions? Does personalized email increase repeat purchases?' These A/B tests inform billions of dollars in product decisions. But most A/B testing is sloppy—misleading results are common. This paper describes the statistical rigor required to trust experiments at scale.
1326.wh: The challenge is that real user populations are not uniform. Some users are mobile-first, others browse on desktop. Some are seasonal (holiday shoppers), others year-round. If you randomly split users into control and test groups without accounting for this heterogeneity, the control and test groups might end up with very different user distributions—one group might get more mobile users, skewing results. Separately, metrics can be too noisy—the real effect might be small, but noise drowns it out, leading you to miss it or falsely claim you found something. Finally, running thousands of concurrent experiments can cause interference: if you're testing checkout flow and payment system simultaneously, it's hard to know which experiment caused the effect.
1326.ap: They apply three statistical techniques in production. First, persona-based stratified assignment: rather than purely random splitting, they partition users into groups based on behavioral patterns, then randomly split within each group—ensuring both the control and test groups have similar distributions of user types. Second, they continuously monitor statistical power (a measure of 'how many users do we need to reliably detect the effect?') and surface it alongside significance, letting experimenters spot underpowered results even when they look statistically significant. Third, orthogonal assignment: when multiple experiments run concurrently, they enforce independence—if experiment A assigns users to version 1 or 2 of checkout, experiment B ensures its assignment doesn't overlap unfairly, so the two experiments don't interfere.
1326.ww: Stratified assignment works because it directly addresses population heterogeneity—if both groups have the same mix of user types, then differences in behavior are due to the treatment, not hidden differences in who joined each group. Continuous power monitoring catches a subtle but common mistake: a result can be 'statistically significant' (p-value < 0.05) but underpowered, meaning the sample size was too small to reliably detect the effect. Orthogonal assignment preserves experimental isolation—if A tests button color and B tests email timing, they should have independent signals, not interfere. Together, these techniques transform A/B testing from a source of false discoveries into a reliable decision mechanism.
1326.po: The payoff is trustworthy experiments that don't mislead product teams. By surfacing power alongside significance and controlling for interference, they reduce false positives (claiming an effect exists when it doesn't) and false negatives (missing real effects). The system enables faster iteration—teams can run many experiments in parallel without fear of cross-contamination—and higher-confidence decisions.

1327.bp: When you shop online and reach the checkout, you see a suggested list of items to add to your order—maybe a matching shirt if you're buying pants, or a wine glass if you're buying wine. This cross-sell basket recommendation is valuable: it increases order size and customer satisfaction. The challenge: with millions of products and complex purchase patterns, how do you predict what each customer will actually want to buy together?
1327.wh: The tension is that purchase history is noisy and biased. If red scarves always show up with red sweaters, it could mean they complement each other—or it could just mean they were displayed next to each other in the store or featured in the same promotion. What looks like 'users who buy scarves also buy sweaters' might be 'users who were shown scarves and sweaters together happen to buy both.' Also, some products are bought together simply because they're popular—not because they genuinely complement each other. Long-tail products (rare items) are under-represented in the data, making recommendations for them almost impossible. And new products have no purchase history at all.
1327.ap: They learn what truly complements what using two tools. First, a debiased scorer aggregates co-purchase history, but with a twist: they weight recent purchases higher than old ones, account for seasonality (some purchases spike in winter), and penalize items that co-occur simply because they're globally popular or over-represented in certain categories. This scorer learns from purchase sequences, extracting genuine complementarity. Second, for items with sparse history (rare and new products), they propagate signals over an item-similarity graph—if product A is similar to product B, and B often ships with product C, then A might ship with C too, even if A is brand-new.
1327.ww: Debiasing works because it explicitly removes the confounding factors—popularity and exposure. If red scarves and red sweaters co-occur in 1,000 transactions, the scorer asks: 'Are they bought together more often than two random popular products? Do they co-occur specifically in red or across all colors?' This reveals true complementarity. The graph propagation handles the long-tail and cold-start problems: if you know 'cashmere is similar to wool' and 'cashmere pairs with certain dyes,' you can infer that wool does too, without needing direct historical evidence. Time and season awareness also matters—holiday gift bundles look different than year-round pairings.
1327.po: In production on a large e-commerce platform, the system shows consistent improvements in predicting future co-purchases offline and maintains robustness even when item distributions are heavily skewed. Online, an A/B test shows statistically significant gains in basket engagement and conversion rates, with positive ripple effects on overall business metrics—users who see good cross-sell recommendations buy more and stay longer.

1328.bp: Enterprise search systems—internal Wikipedia for a company, document search for a legal firm—need to find relevant files fast and store data efficiently. Modern search uses neural networks to turn text into numbers (an embedding), then compares embeddings to find matches. The challenge: smaller, faster models (which run on cheap hardware) often perform worse than large models (which need expensive GPUs). Can you build compact embedding models that still perform well?
1328.wh: Creating good text embeddings requires scale—training on billions of text pairs to learn what makes two texts similar. Shrinking a model (fewer parameters, smaller memory footprint) usually means sacrificing that learned knowledge. You lose the nuanced understanding of language that large models built up. So companies face a trade-off: pay for expensive large models to run inference, or use cheaper small models and get worse search results. Another tension: embeddings need to stay robust when quantized (compressed to fewer bits for storage), but quantization erases fine details that small models depend on.
1328.ap: They train small embedding models using distillation—a technique where a large, well-trained teacher model guides a small student model. The key insight: rather than training the student on generic data, they use task-specific contrastive losses, meaning they train the student on pairs of texts that are relevant to specific use cases (legal documents, financial reports, medical texts). They also add a regularization strategy designed specifically to make embeddings robust to binary quantization—essentially training the model to keep important information in just a few high-value bits, rather than spreading information across many dimensions.
1328.ww: Distillation works because the large teacher model already knows what good embeddings look like; the student learns by copying that knowledge. Task-specific losses then sharpen the student: instead of learning a generic 'similarity' concept, it learns 'what makes two medical documents related?' and 'what makes two financial documents related?', making it more useful for real enterprise applications. Quantization-aware regularization is clever because it acknowledges that small models will be quantized and trains them accordingly, rather than naively compressing a model trained for full precision.
1328.po: The result is compact models small enough to run on modest hardware, deployable in resource-constrained settings (phones, embedded systems, edge servers), that match or surpass the quality of existing models of the same size. Since weights are publicly released, researchers can build on this work without spending weeks training large models.

1329.bp: On e-commerce sites, when you search for 'wool blazer size 12 navy,' you're expressing multiple specific desires: you want wool (not polyester), size 12 (not 14), and navy (not charcoal). A good search system should match all three. But many systems only generate a single query embedding and a single product embedding, then score their similarity. This is efficient but crude—it can't check whether the product actually satisfies all your attribute requirements.
1329.wh: Aggregate representations (one number per query, one per product) have a fundamental limitation: they squash all information into a single score, so they can't distinguish whether the product matches some attributes but not others. Example: you search 'wool blazer navy' and get back a 'polyester blazer navy'—semantically similar (both are blazers, both navy), but it misses your wool requirement because the aggregate score only sees the overall semantic match, not the attribute-level match. Fine-grained methods that check attribute-by-attribute exist, but they're slow—checking every attribute for every candidate product is expensive at scale. You want to keep the speed of aggregate matching while adding attribute-level precision.
1329.ap: They design a system that works in stages. First, a query processing stage extracts and canonicalizes attributes from the user's search: 'wool' (material), 'size 12' (size), 'navy' (color). They map these to a structured database of known attributes. Second, they learn a model that scores granular attribute affinity—for each attribute, how well does this product match the user's intent? Third, they compute an aggregate score by combining these per-attribute scores. Crucially, they design the system to run efficiently in production: they pre-compute and cache attribute-level matches so online inference doesn't pay a penalty for fine-grainedness.
1329.ww: Attribute-level decomposition works because it makes explicit what matters: if the user specified 'wool,' that's a hard constraint for many shoppers, and the system should respect it. By scoring attribute-by-attribute, the model can learn 'material attribute mismatches are costly' while 'style mismatches are less critical.' Pre-computation and caching are crucial for efficiency—you don't compute attribute matches on-the-fly; you compute them once and store them, so online queries are still fast. This preserves the scalability of two-tower retrieval (where query and product are separate) while adding fine-grained intent checking.
1329.po: The system substantially improves satisfaction of explicit user intent—users searching for 'wool' get wool items, not just semantically similar non-wool items—while maintaining the speed and scalability of large-scale e-commerce. Experiments show real improvements in relevance metrics sensitive to attribute matching, benefiting both broad queries (where attribute intent is clear) and tail queries (where few candidates match anyway, so precision is critical).

1330.bp: Scientific peer review is central to deciding which papers get published, which ideas matter, which researchers earn credibility. Yet peer review is largely opaque and unevaluated—there's no systematic audit of review quality. In 2025-2026, large language models are increasingly used by reviewers: to draft reviews, restructure arguments, or polish prose. This creates a new transparency crisis: how much of a review is human reasoning versus AI-generated text? Is the core intellectual contribution from the human or the model?
1330.wh: The challenge is distinguishing human thinking from AI-assisted writing without a ground-truth label. A reviewer might have read the paper, identified three key weaknesses, then asked an LLM to 'write a professional-sounding paragraph about these weaknesses.' The ideas are human; the text is AI-generated. Or the opposite: an LLM might draft a review, and the human reviewer just adds a few touches. Authorship detection alone (using tools that flag AI-written text) isn't enough—you need to know whether the intellectual contribution is human, not just count the AI-generated sentences. Also, reviews need other quality dimensions: Are the criticisms grounded in evidence from the paper? Do claims match the manuscript's actual content, or is the reviewer hallucinating?
1330.ap: They build three tools. Peeriscope evaluates review quality across interpretable dimensions (depth, constructiveness, specificity, etc.). Peerispect uses retrieval-augmented generation—it takes reviewer claims and checks them against the manuscript text, retrieving relevant passages to verify whether the claims are actually supported. PeerPrism analyzes hybrid authorship by disentangling where ideas originate (human reasoning or model suggestion?) from where text originates (human-written or AI-generated?). They treat these as separate axes—allowing measurement of collaboration intensity.
1330.ww: Retrieval-based verification works because it grounds abstract claims in concrete evidence. When a reviewer writes 'the paper lacks baseline comparisons,' Peerispect retrieves the methods and results sections of the manuscript to check whether baselines are actually missing. Hybrid authorship analysis works by tracing the ideational origin of statements (Does this idea align with what a reasoning LLM would suggest?) separately from textual origin (Is this phrasing characteristic of the reviewer's writing or of LLMs?). This nuance is crucial: hybrid workflows aren't inherently bad—they can improve clarity—but transparency requires measuring the degree of collaboration.
1330.po: The payoff is infrastructure for auditing peer review at scale. Reviewerly's deployed systems give stakeholders—journals, conferences, institutions—a way to measure review quality and detect problematic patterns: reviews that make unsupported claims, reviews that are largely AI-generated without human reasoning, reviews that aren't constructive. This supports both accountability (bad reviewers can be identified) and transparency (readers can understand how much human expertise went into a review's reasoning).

1331.bp: When you search a large database, two broad strategies compete: sparse retrieval (keyword matching—if the query says 'machine learning,' find documents with those words) and dense retrieval (semantic matching—find documents about learning systems even if they don't use those exact words). Sparse is fast and interpretable; dense is more accurate. Hybrid systems combine both, but they often don't work well together. This paper asks: how do you make sparse and dense signals truly interact?
1331.wh: The problem is that sparse and dense signals can conflict. A document might match the query keywords perfectly but be semantically unrelated (a restaurant review mentioning 'machine learning' restaurant name). A dense model might score it high because it caught the words; a sparse model might score it high for the same reason. But they're solving different problems: sparse finds keyword matches; dense finds semantic matches. If you just add the scores together, they don't reinforce each other intelligently—you get interference rather than fusion. Under intersection-based retrieval (where you filter to documents that match both keyword and semantic criteria), the benefits of hybridization are limited because the filtering itself is already restrictive.
1331.ap: They build a unified encoder with a shared backbone—one neural network that learns both lexical (word-level) and semantic (meaning-level) representations jointly. Rather than training them separately then combining scores, they co-train: both representations are learned from the same data with aligned objectives. They also add hybrid score regularization (a penalty that encourages the two scores to be consistent if the document is truly relevant) and consistency distillation (training the model to produce similar scores from the two signals). This ensures that lexical and semantic agreement becomes a sign of strong relevance.
1331.ww: Joint training works because it lets the model learn how to make lexical and semantic representations work together, not just coexist. A shared backbone means both representations are built on the same foundation, so they inherit correlated structure. Score regularization adds an explicit signal: if a document is truly relevant (high quality), its sparse and dense scores should align; if they diverge, something is likely wrong. This catches false positives—documents that score well on keywords but semantically miss the mark. Consistency distillation uses this alignment as a training target, further tightening integration.
1331.po: On public benchmarks, HybridSparse consistently beats pure sparse, pure dense, and naive hybrid baselines. In large-scale production deployment for Bing advertisement retrieval (millions of queries daily, billions of ads to search), the system delivers a 1.30 percent RPM (revenue per mille) gain—a significant impact on ad ranking, the most critical signal in search.

1332.bp: Large language model agents—AI systems that break down problems into steps, call tools, and refine answers—perform much better than raw language models on complex tasks. But building a capable agent for each user request is expensive and unstable: you need to dynamically compose expert roles, set up memories, choose tools, which requires computing resources and introduces failure points. This paper asks: what if you precomputed thousands of agent configurations and just retrieved the right one for each query?
1332.wh: The tension is cost versus flexibility. A fully dynamic agent system (designing agents on-the-fly for each query) is slow—you need to prompt the LLM to decide roles, then instantiate them, then run inference. It's also fragile—the LLM might make bad architectural choices for the task. A precomputed library of agents is fast and stable, but how do you build and organize it? Do you precompute every possible agent? How do you match a new query to the right precomputed agent? Will a generic library of agents actually match the nuance of what a specific user needs?
1332.ap: They build LLM Agents Factory: a library of over 20,000 predetermined agent profiles, each with specific expertise (a medical expert, a coding expert, an essay-writing expert). These agents are grounded in Wikipedia, so their roles and knowledge are verifiable. They then support two retrieval modes: (1) semantic search—when a query arrives, retrieve the most similar agent profile from the library; (2) distillation—train a smaller model to directly generate agents from scratch, but initializing from the library so it stays grounded. Experiments on standardized benchmarks compare these to non-agentic approaches and to dynamic agent generation (AutoGen).
1332.ww: Retrieval from a pre-built library works because human-designed agents (or agents that have been refined once and stored) tend to be better than on-the-fly designs. The library size (20K agents) is large enough to cover diverse domains but small enough to be manageable. Semantic search quickly finds the agent type relevant to a query. The distillation mode adds flexibility: if no precomputed agent perfectly matches, a trained model can generate a new one, but it's initialized from the library, so it stays reasonable. Wikipedia grounding ensures agents have factual knowledge, not just role names.
1332.po: On standardized benchmarks (MMLU, BIG-Bench), retrieval-based agent construction matches AutoGen (a leading dynamic agent framework) in accuracy while being substantially cheaper to run—no need to prompt for on-the-fly agent design for every query. The system is production-ready: cost-efficient, accurate, and controllable, responding to industrial demands for reliable AI agents without astronomical inference costs.

1333.bp: Imagine you're a restaurant owner on a delivery app, and the company wants to predict the impact of raising prices by 10 percent, or expanding hours, or running a promotion. You can't run these experiments on real customers without risk—maybe a price increase crushes orders and revenue drops. A simulator that predicts how customers would react to your strategy changes would let you make smarter decisions safely. This paper builds such a simulator for merchants on Meituan, a major Chinese platform.
1333.wh: Simulating user behavior is hard because real user decisions depend on unobserved factors—offline context (the weather that day), implicit habits (I always order Thai on Thursdays), social influence (my friends recommend this place). A pure reasoning-based approach (ask an LLM 'if this restaurant raised prices, would you order?') over-rationalizes—it invents explanations for decisions without access to the messy reality of how people actually choose. A pure statistical approach (fitting curves to historical data) works for predicting what users will do, but can't explain the causal impact of changing one variable. You need both explanatory reasoning and empirical prediction together.
1333.ap: They build a dual-process framework: an LLM-based reasoning branch and an ML-based statistical branch, aligned by learned decision policies. The first step mines decision policies from user behavioral trajectories—what explicit rules do users follow? ('If price > $X, they don't order.'). These policies become a shared layer that anchors both processes. The reasoning branch uses these policies to structure its causal reasoning, preventing over-rationalization. The statistical branch uses them to ground its predictions in observed patterns. Group-level predictions from both branches are then combined—if both agree a merchant should expect fewer orders after a price increase, they weight that prediction higher; if they disagree, they blend the signals.
1333.ww: This works because decision policies act as a bridge between causal reasoning and statistical fitting. Policies are extracted from data (empirical) but can be articulated (interpretable), so they ground the LLM's reasoning in observed behavior rather than unconstrained speculation. The LLM can then reason about counterfactuals ('if we raise price, which policies activate?') without over-inventing explanations. The statistical model learns the residual patterns that policies don't capture (the implicit regularities). By fusing predictions at the group level (not individual level), the system reduces variance—group-level trends are more stable than individual predictions.
1333.po: Deployed on a real platform (Meituan, 101 merchants, 26K+ trajectories), the system achieves 8.80 percent group-level simulation error, beating reasoning-only and fitting-only baselines by 45.8 percent and 40.9 percent respectively. This enables merchants to safely explore counterfactual strategies before deploying changes, improving decision quality without expensive online experimentation.

1334.bp: On e-commerce platforms like Walmart, predicting what users will add to their cart is more nuanced than simple relevance. When someone searches 'steak,' they probably want beef steak, not equally relevant pork or ostrich steak—they have implicit preferences shaped by culture, past purchases, and what they've learned about quality. Building a search system that captures these implicit preferences is crucial for engagement, basket size, and customer satisfaction.
1334.wh: The tension is that traditional relevance models miss implicit intent. If you ask 'is this steak relevant to the query steak?', both beef and pork are yes—they're both steaks. But users have preferences beyond relevance. One approach is to mine historical engagement data: 'which products do users add-to-cart after this search?' But this fails for new products and tail queries (rare searches with sparse data). Another approach is to use query-level intent signals, but these are noisy and coarse—they average over thousands of users with different preferences.
1334.ap: They extend a BERT-based cross-encoder (a model that reads query and item text together and scores relevance) to predict engagement directly. Rather than predicting relevance, the model learns from query-item text with engagement labels—actual add-to-cart behavior. The cross-encoder architecture means the model sees the query and item text side-by-side and learns fine-grained interactions: why does 'ribeye' plus 'grass-fed' plus 'premium' engagement-signal together, but 'sirloin' plus 'frozen' doesn't? This fine-grained learning captures the implicit preferences baked into user behavior across diverse query types.
1334.ww: Learning from engagement labels (actual add-to-cart actions) rather than relevance labels works because it directly optimizes for user behavior. The cross-encoder architecture is crucial—it can capture nuanced query-item interactions that simple retrieval can't. For tail queries where historical engagement signals are sparse, the model generalizes from text: if similar terms appear in queries that historically led to engagement, it learns to weight them similarly. This is more robust than trying to memorize engagement statistics.
1334.po: Deployed at Walmart, the model shows +1.71 percent lift in add-to-cart rate in interleaving tests (where the system randomly shows old vs. new ranking to A/B test), and +0.33 percent across overall search sessions. These gains compound: more add-to-carts mean higher order values and session engagement. The model succeeds across the board—tail queries (where old approaches failed due to sparse data) benefit from the learned semantic understanding, and broad queries benefit from fine-grained intent capture.
